extracted.intended_audience: trainers of college mathematics instructors; instructional consultants and faculty developers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and running instructor-training meetings and programs of classroom observation (including scheduling visits, collecting feedback, videotape/peer review, and facilitation of meetings) aimed at improving college mathematics teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule classroom visits early and provide constructive feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a schedule of visits and feedback affords the most personalized support ... trainers should plan to do them early in the semester, and they should be well prepared, supportive, credible, and thorough in their feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visits are most worthwhile when done early; visits should not be used for evaluation purposes only; trainers should be well prepared, supportive, credible, and thorough to obtain maximum benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use detailed observation checklists (Weimer et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: An extensive checklist intended for use by classroom observers with questions arranged into categories: importance and suitability of content, organization of content, presentation style, establishing and maintaining contact with students, and questioning ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such checklists to rate instructor, students and general features of the class; adapt items to local context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing assessment and feedback cycle (Weimer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situate ongoing assessment within a five step plan: develop instructional awareness, gather information, decide what to change and how to change it, implement changes, and assess effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple approaches to assess teaching; enshrine feedback as part of a continuous improvement cycle rather than a one-off judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt rubrics for professional standards (Baiocco & DeWaters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four rubrics listed as planning and organization, classroom management, methods and techniques, and personal, with lists of criteria beneath each reflecting high standards of professional conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubrics give concrete criteria but beware decontextualized formulations (e.g., 'use of the board was very effective') — adapt and specify what evidence observers should look for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect midsemester student feedback using SGID
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Small Group Instructional Diagnosis (SGID) or similar small-group student feedback procedures for collecting midterm feedback; SGID reported positive student responses and improved motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SGID emphasizes consensus-building and can be a useful alternative to end-of-semester questionnaires; implementation details and appendices may be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe key classroom interaction quantities (Mitsakos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe: the amount of time students spend working on learning tasks, the amount of teacher talking, the amount and quality of student–teacher and student–student interaction, and the teacher's classroom management skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate observation techniques with the instructor beforehand; select methods targeted to phenomena of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a pre-visit conference to clarify instructor intentions (Sorcinelli)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult with the teacher before observations; use pre-visit questions to draw instructors out and develop a clear picture of intended class activities and areas for feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sorcinelli suggests eight pre-visit questions and a post-observation interview; tailor rubrics to the instructor's model of teaching when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rubrics tied to teaching excellence (Sorcinelli)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested rubrics include: knowledge of the subject matter, organization and clarity, instructor–student interaction (including use of questions), presentation and enthusiasm, and student behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rubrics are tied to a particular model of excellence; adapt to institutional context and clarify observable evidence for each rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ethnographic observation methods for in-depth study (Frank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply ethnographic lenses to see classroom culture, reading between the lines of classroom events; suitable for intensive, ongoing observation focused on patterns and culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods assume in-depth, long-term observation and may be less useful for large-scale GSI development but valuable for single-course, intensive improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate videotape as a self-evaluation tool (Davis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use videotape primarily for instructor self-evaluation with a clear procedure for recording and analyzing one's class: view soon after recording, spend about twice as long analyzing as the class length, view with a supportive colleague, start with big-picture impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After big-picture viewing, re-view to focus on specifics (frequency/type of interactions, questions, voice/body language). Use Davis's checklist areas such as organization, style, clarity, questioning skills, student interest, and classroom climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Videotape multiple times (Hamkins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend taping GSIs twice per semester; the first taping may reveal little (self-consciousness), the second taping often reveals more authentic teaching behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule repeated recordings to allow instructors to acclimate and for progress to be visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer visits and mixed-discipline observer teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer visits involve faculty visiting each other's classes and offering feedback; teams of observers can include mathematicians and faculty from other disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer visits can supplement videotape and foster discussion; include diverse perspectives where useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to hold a meeting at all
rubrics_metrics.description: Before planning or announcing a meeting, ask 'Do we really need to have a meeting at all?' If information can be conveyed equally effectively by other means, consider alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives include email, individual interviews, or small-group meetings; be respectful of participants' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop clear meeting objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Trainers should develop objectives or goals for the instructors involved in their training program to determine whether a meeting is required and what it should accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: help instructors become proficient at grading homework; define use of quizzes in grading; surface difficult classroom situations; ensure syllabus coverage before exams. Objectives can be addressed in full meetings or via other venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Key organizational criteria: trainers have clear objectives, an agenda is prepared in advance, participants can contribute to the agenda if appropriate, meeting time/day suits participants, participants receive notice in advance, and decide which items can be omitted if time runs over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and circulate agendas well in advance; specify preparatory work expected of participants; identify items that can be deferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The meeting room should be large enough and accommodate planned activities (small groups, etc.), have comfortable temperature, access to restrooms/refreshments for long meetings, and working audiovisual equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rooms that facilitate planned activities; consider room layout for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time management: start and end on time
rubrics_metrics.description: The meeting begins and ends on time; leaders monitor time throughout and try to stick to the schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide in advance which agenda items can be lightened or omitted; balance allowing work time with keeping the meeting on schedule; END THE MEETING ON TIME!

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote balanced participation
rubrics_metrics.description: If appropriate, everyone has a chance to present views, periodic summaries are used, no one dominates, and everyone has a voice if decisions are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use facilitation techniques to draw out quieter participants and prevent domination; summarize progress periodically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign and enforce responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should be reliable in carrying out agreed actions; instructors attend; meeting leader follows up on unanswered questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulate a customized list of criteria for meeting effectiveness to participants; follow-up is part of meeting accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address common meeting complaints proactively
rubrics_metrics.description: Common complaints include drifting off subject, poor preparation, questionable effectiveness, lack of listening, verbosity, length, and lack of participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address these via objectives, agendas, time management, participant selection, leadership, and summarizing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only meet if absolutely necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If other possibilities achieve objectives (email, interviews, small groups), use them instead of large meetings to respect participants' time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat meetings as results of decision-making rather than default actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and circulate an agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: The agenda tells participants what to expect, how meeting time will be used, and appropriate forms/levels of participation; distribute well in advance and indicate required preparations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the agenda to guide discussion back on track when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective about participants when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller numbers often increase engagement, while more people increase perspective; invite those who will benefit (e.g., struggling instructors) and consider private outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance inclusivity with effectiveness; target attendance to meeting goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take charge of the meeting when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders must manage time, keep discussion on topic, prevent domination or off-topic wandering, and ensure the meeting ends on time. Choose a leadership style you can use effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to stop meetings or change the format if needed; enforce ground rules respectfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: End meetings with a summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Reiterate goals and review suggested changes or actions; a sincere pep talk may help but insincerity can backfire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summaries should be concrete and review follow-up actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulate discussion by planned questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting leaders should use purposeful questions to encourage participation: ask for opinions, call on people by name, request summaries, clarify statements, ask for examples, look for differences, explore details, protect participants, question assumptions, and look ahead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unanswerable questions, yes/no questions, vague questions, and interrogations. Ensure discussions are not simply leader–participant Q&A sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange physical layout to encourage discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Room layout affects discussion: seating participants facing each other encourages discussion more than lecture-style seating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rooms or layouts that facilitate planned meeting activities when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define clear roles: leader, participant, facilitator, recorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Meetings work best when everyone has a clear role. Leader focuses on content and meeting ownership; participant prepares and contributes; facilitator manages process and neutrality; recorder captures ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute role responsibilities in advance so participants know expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader's responsibilities: preparation and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare objectives and agenda, schedule and invite attendees, circulate agenda, ensure people know roles, prepare materials, check room/equipment; start meeting on time, state goals, establish ground rules, follow agenda, summarize key points, and end on time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leader may need to stop the meeting and change format; ensure logistics are handled beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant's responsibilities: preparation and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should review the agenda, confirm attendance, do required preparation, know objectives, arrive on time, keep an open mind, help ensure broad participation, stick to agenda items, suggest alternatives, share useful ideas, and support ground rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulate participant responsibilities before meetings; address persistent noncompliance if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitator's responsibilities: process management
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitator develops objectives with leader, reviews agenda, helps with logistics, reads the plan, anticipates difficult situations; during the meeting focuses participants, stimulates discussion, gets everyone to participate, monitors time, protects people/ideas, deals with difficult people, remains neutral, and keeps small groups productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a facilitator distinct from the content leader when conflicts may involve the leader or policies they advocate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recorder's responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Recorder reviews agenda beforehand, confirms attendance, prepares as required; during the meeting captures ideas without editing, checks for recording accuracy, and helps keep track of accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recorders when meetings need an accurate, neutral account of proceedings; otherwise leader may handle note-taking for brief meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deal with difficult situations and people using interpersonal skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting leaders must manage side conversations, dominance, lack of contribution, and other interpersonal problems through interpersonal control and facilitation techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train leaders in interpersonal skills (e.g., Carnegie); identify common problems and apply adapted remedies (see A.6).
